content: Polygonatum, commonly known as King Solomon's Seal or Solomon's Seal, is a genus comprising approximately 50 species of flowering plants within the family Ruscaceae. Previously, these plants were classified under the lily family, Liliaceae. Certain species within this genus possess medicinal properties, and some, particularly Polygonatum sibiricum, are utilized in traditional Chinese medicine as a tisane. In Korea, this tisane is referred to as Duong Gul Le. The shoots of some Polygonatum species are edible and can be prepared in a manner similar to asparagus. Additionally, the roots, after undergoing appropriate treatment, are also consumable and serve as a rich source of starch. The medicinal applications of Solomon's Seal primarily revolve around its root. Traditionally, it has been employed to address a variety of conditions, ranging from menopausal symptoms to the treatment of broken bones. When applied topically, the root is believed to expedite the healing of cuts, bruises, skin irritations, and inflammations. It is also used as a facial wash to treat acne, blemishes, and other skin imperfections. When consumed as a tea, Solomon's Seal is said to alleviate a wide range of symptoms, including those associated with menopause, indigestion, diabetes, broken bones, insomnia, kidney pain, and even infertility. Its potential in combating diabetes was first observed in 1930 by Langecker. Through his experiments, he concluded that it was effective in addressing nutritional hyperglycemia, though it did not appear to counteract hyperglycemia caused by adrenaline release. This effect is thought to be linked to its glucokinin content.
